​“I think that O Canada is a good national anthem among the slightly underrated ones, including the Thai and the Vatican anthems,” @jerskinfendrix tells @t.s.waite in the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine. ⁠
⁠
The classically trained, experimental pop musician released his last album, Once Upon a Time ... in Shropshire, in 2025, and has produced sweeping, avant-garde scores for several films by Yorgos Lanthimos, including last year’s Bugonia. “I looked [the anthem] up recently because it was referenced on Shoresy, a Canadian comedy show by Jared Keeso, and I found O Canada! – an album of 22 recordings of the anthem, arranged for orchestra, marching band, organ, carillon and children’s choir, in French, English and bilingual versions. I spent a lot of days on the road playing it on repeat – it becomes a hypnotic joke. I can only assume it was intended to be an encyclopedic album, which is so formally weird.”⁠

“As an artist, I find it impossible to view my photographs objectively,” @divola writes in the afterword of his new photo book, Sheila. ⁠
⁠
The book is named for Divola’s former wife, whose recurring presence is its guiding principle. In an email conversation, Divola tells @ohnoitsemilyd he wouldn’t describe Sheila as a love story. “First, the book is not a biography. Sheila and I have decided that we don’t want a dialogue around the book to be engaged in that manner.” Yet in his afterword, the photographer offers this tantalising insight: “I first met Sheila sometime in 1975. I fell hopelessly and deeply in love – the kind of love that inhabits one’s whole physical, emotional and intellectual being. A love you read about in books but assume is an exaggeration.” While the configuration of photographs in Sheila defies a kind of linear biographical reading, each image is a souvenir; a postcard from a moment in time. Japanese novelist Yukio Mishima was a five-time Nobel Prize for Literature nominee whose strict dedication to traditional values often combated with his lush language and exploration of repressed sexuality. A controversial literary figure, Mishima first came across photographer Eikoh Hosoe through his images of the legendary butoh dancer Tatsumi Hijikata – the latter had interpreted the writer’s own homoerotic novel Kinjiki in 1959 in what is now considered the first genuine butoh dance. ⁠
⁠
Mishima – a champion of traditionalist cultural values whose novels and stories often dealt with closeted protagonists’ struggles to fit into post-war Japanese society – saw in Hosoe a young avant-garde artist coming of age in the shadow of the Japan-US war and its aftermath, and immediately felt drawn to become the subject of his photography.⁠
⁠
The result was the photographic series, Barakei (Ordeal by Roses). The new exhibition, Props from Barakei, at the @leslielohmanmuseum, brings together around 20 of Hosoe’s black and white photographs of Mishima from the series alongside a mixed-media installation of ropes, swords and a camera by Berlin and Singapore-based contemporary artist and poet Jason Wee.⁠
⁠
At the link in bio, @osmancanyerebakan speaks with @nakamoriyasufumi, the show’s curator about the “tension” between Mishima and Hosoe, two 20th-century Japanese figures who represent seemingly opposing social values 📲⁠

The star-studded presentation also featured Kate Moss, Helena Christensen, Karen Mulder, Carla Bruni, Carmen Dell’Orefice, and Shalom Harlow, culminating in a playful finale where models tossed confetti across the runway.

Dior Homme Fall/Winter 2004/05 “Victim of the Crime” by Hedi Slimane.

Marking a decisive pivot from his earlier electronic/Berlin club references toward mid-2000s indie rock androgyny, FW04 took its unofficial title from Phoenix’s original runway soundtrack, “Victim of the Crime.”

Built around a reimagined traditional “vestiaire,” Slimane systematically shrunk classic menswear archetypes trench coats, duffle coats, varsity jackets, and biker silhouettes, cutting them high in the armhole and cropped at the waist to achieve what he termed a “suspended posture and allure.”

Two years ago, Jacqui Hooper (@jacquilouise__) had never given modelling a serious thought. She was a dancer from Southampton, studying criminology and forensic psychology at university.

Everything changed on a rainy day at Reading Festival. A scout from Next spotted her in the crowd, and months later she made her runway debut at Versace in Milan. Since then Jacquie has walked for Chanel, fronted campaigns for Prada, Chloé and McQueen, and industry leaders voted her as the breakout model of 2025 on models.com.

So how does a newcomer learn to navigate a notoriously tough industry? For Hooper, it comes down to reading the room.

“Some people will be really complimentary of you the entire time, and then as soon as those compliments stop coming as fast, you’re like, ‘Okay, so this isn’t what they want – clearly I need to change something here,’” Hooper recalls. “It’s usually when people get quiet that I’m like, ‘Okay, I need to change this.’”

This week, Hooper joins @ImranAmed in our London office to talk about what it really takes to make it as a model today, the growing expectation that models double as content creators, and why she’d rather not “sing about it on Instagram.”

i’ve always been a firm believer in fashion collaborations. i remember watching the karl lagerfeld x h&m ad on youtube (it had already sold out by then) and obsessing over it. (it remains one of the best fashion ad films ever made btw.) i bought mugler x h&m because i absolutely loved casey cadwallader’s work, and that was the only way i could afford it.

and that’s the beauty of collaborations. they bring different worlds together, introduce brands to new audiences, make otherwise inaccessible designers a little more accessible. great marketing, great PR, great business. and when done right can be exciting.

but 2026 has felt so mechanical. something that once felt like a rare cultural moment now feels like a weekly marketing exercise. at this point, it’s probably harder to find two brands that haven’t collaborated.

sure, etro x birkenstock gave us some beautiful products. zuhair murad x aldo felt very on-brand. but then there’s rimowa x margiela, which genuinely traumatised me. elie saab x h&m? still doesn’t make sense to me. ganni x lululemon….ugly, sorry.

and i think there’s a bigger conversation here about the difference between commercial success and cultural relevance.

a collaboration might get someone to buy from a brand for the first time, but are they actually buying into that brand, or just the name it’s collaborating with? and once the hype dies down, what reason have you given that customer to come back?

you can find a clever brand rationale for almost any partnership. but clever doesn’t necessarily mean compelling. and selling out a collection doesn’t automatically mean you’ve created something culturally meaningful. i think 2026 has really exposed just how formulaic fashion collaborations have become. 

have fashion collaborations reached their saturation point? what do u think?

"Curtains make people behave very differently," said Louise Giovanelli.

The young British painter has seen it first-hand. Her life-size oil paintings of undulating drapes, where folds of velvet or tinsel absorb and refract the glow of a stage spotlight, often become the backdrop for visitor selfies when her work is shown in galleries across the UK, New York, Amsterdam and Munich. "People always go and take selfies in front of the curtains," she said. "They don't do it in front of any other painting."

In the last five years, the 33-year-old has become an art world bright spot for her ominous, radiant drapes painted Old Masters-style with slow, painstaking brushwork. Ahead of her new London show, "In the Light of False Suns" at the White Cube gallery in central London, Giovanelli unpacks what makes her work so hypnotic — and the one question you should never ask her.

📸: DACS 2026/Theo Christelis/White Cube

In this week’s edition of “Big Style,” guest writer Glynnis MacNicol, @noonetellsyouthis, is talking about the power of a fur coat — and she’s delving into the archives to find the women who wore them best. In the 1990s, Jil Sander revolutionized fashion advertising by stripping away commercial slogans, theatrical sets, and overt glamour in favor of stark, conceptual minimalism. Known as the “Queen of Less,” Sander translated her pure, architectural tailoring directly onto the printed page, creating campaigns that looked more like fine-art exhibition catalogues than traditional luxury ads.

To celebrate Letterman’s 48th birthday—and after chatting about her recent wild-child antics—the actress spontaneously climbed onto his desk, danced with her back to the cameras, and briefly lifted her top to flash him. A visibly stunned Letterman famously reacted by saying, „I can’t thank you enough for that“. The unscripted stunt instantly became a defining pop-culture moment of the 1990s.

Spanning twelve pages, photographer Juergen Teller captured a 21-year-old Kate Moss far removed from artificial sets. Sliding Doors is a 1998 romantic drama directed by Peter Howitt and starring Gwyneth Paltrow as Helen Quilley, a London public relations executive. The film follows two parallel timelines depending on whether Helen catches or misses a London Underground train after being fired. Beyond its inventive split-narrative plot, the movie has become a lasting fashion reference point for late-90s minimalism.
To give Helen a timeless look rather than one tied to fleeting trends, costume designer Jill Taylor worked with a limited budget and turned directly to Calvin Klein. Because Gwyneth Paltrow was already a close friend and muse of the designer, she and Taylor were granted access to the Calvin Klein showroom. There, they sourced the core of Helen’s on-screen wardrobe, selecting signature pieces like wide-leg trousers, fine-knit turtlenecks, sleek leather outerwear, and understated basics.
Taylor blended these Calvin Klein pieces with a few items from Prada, secondhand finds, and garments from her own closet to make the styling feel effortless and authentic. Because the outfits rely on clean tailoring and neutral silhouettes, they visually distinguish Helen’s evolving confidence across both storylines without ever looking dated. Today, the film serves as a curated archive of authentic 1990s Calvin Klein minimalism.

In 1987, a 17-year-old Claudia Schiffer walked into a nightclub in Düsseldorf, Germany, hoping to study law and work at her father’s firm. Instead, she caught the eye of a modeling agency boss, a chance encounter that instantly changed the trajectory of fashion history.

Within just a few years, the shy teenager transformed into one of the most recognizable faces on the planet. Handpicked by Karl Lagerfeld to become the face of Chanel, Schiffer quickly rose to the top of the 1990s supermodel era alongside peers like Cindy Crawford and Naomi Campbell.

Her impact on pop culture was unmatched. Throughout her career, Schiffer appeared on more than 1,000 magazine covers, a feat that earned her a place in the Guinness Book of World Records. Decades later, she remains a timeless symbol of 90s glamour and one of the most successful models the industry has ever seen.

In April 1996, Gillian Anderson appeared in FHM magazine’s editorial “Close Encounters”, accompanied by an extensive interview by journalist Anthony Noguera. At the time, Anderson was internationally recognised for her role as FBI Special Agent Dana Scully in The X-Files, which had become one of television’s biggest cultural phenomena of the 1990s.

The editorial offered a very different image of the actress from the one audiences were used to seeing on screen. While Scully was known for her practical FBI suits, oversized coats and understated appearance, the photographs presented Anderson in a more glamorous and provocative setting. The shoot included several different looks, among them black lingerie, a man’s shirt and a striking blue catsuit. Anderson was also photographed in a series of playful poses involving handcuffs, deliberately distancing herself from her television character.

The accompanying interview explored the contrast between Anderson and the character that had made her famous. She spoke about her unexpected status as a sex symbol, her unconventional teenage years, her early experiences in theatre and the pressures of working on The X-Files. The feature was particularly significant because it presented her as a personality in her own right, rather than simply as Dana Scully.

The issue became a major success for FHM and was later described by the magazine’s features editor as its fastest-selling issue at the time. It also helped introduce a different side of Anderson to the public, beyond her now-iconic television role.

“Dare I say you were sort-of, like, torched,” Sorkin said. 

“Torched,” Bieber replied. 

She went on to admit that she used “definitely the wrong word,” and explained that “at Rhode we really do have a very curated and edited SKU count in comparison to most traditional beauty brands, and our drop cadence is a lot slower and spread out [sic] than most other traditional beauty brands. The original ‘overconsumption’ comment sparked fierce backlash in October after Bieber spoke at Fortune’s Most Powerful Women Summit. Audiences called her out for selling pimple patch cases, cheap bag charms, and phone cases that hold lip gloss tubes.

The actual worth of luxury products is sometimes hard to put your finger on; How do you determine the price of exclusivity? And how do you maintain it? The answer is almost never to lower the price—in fact, that’s antithetical to maintaining a product’s aura of exclusivity. But that’s what Gucci is doing, as many customers have recently realized. 

Gucci has suffered 13 consecutive quarters of underperforming sales, and now something has got to give. In August, Kering’s CEO Luca de Meo admitted that price hikes may have gone further than was necessary, and that “corrections” may be in the future.

“We are fully aware that the market will not allow us to pass our inefficiencies on to customers,” he added.

“Inefficiencies” and “corrections” are rather vague jargon words that tip-toe around an uglier truth: some luxury items may not be worth what we’ve been told they are. The public is starting to notice that some carryover styles like tshirts, sneakers, and handbags have decreased in price up to 30%. A suede Beatrix tote bag, for example, decreased in price from $3300 to $2310.

But Gucci is not the only brand struggling to appeal to its target market of aspirational middle-class customers. LVMH executives and investors are reportedly “debating” the possibility of similar cuts at Louis Vuitton in response to the brand’s falling sales. LVMH, though, is resistant to the price-cut option, which the Wall Street Journal called “striking.” Are price cuts really the nuclear option for struggling luxury brands? Even for brands that used to incinerate merchandise to maintain the aura of exclusivity?

For years, luxury brands have set prices higher and higher, whether it was to distance themselves from increasingly uncanny dupes or to remain on the rich side of ever-widening wealth gaps. But now, customers seem to have seized an ounce (at best 30%) of their power back; Don’t cave for ridiculous price hikes and the price may stop hiking. Either that, or we’re truly in the recession they keep telling us we’re not in.

Robert Pattinson is on a generational run. The 40-year old British actor was just announced as the new James Bond.

This is no ordinary casting; Bond is a serious commitment due to its extremely devoted fanbase, its decades of lore, the formulaic system within which it operates, and the physical expectations required of its actors. Does Pattinson fit the bill?

On the page, not exactly. For starters, Bond’s are typically molded from lesser-known actors so the face of the MI6 agent is as mysterious to audiences as possible. The former Bond, Daniel Craig, was far from a leading man before taking on the role. And Sean Connery was a bodybuilder before being cast. Pattinson will be the first Bond who we’ve known by a handful of other iconic names, such as Bruce Wayne or Edward Cullen. That’s saying nothing of his much discussed roles in less blockbuster-y, more artsy films like ‘Lighthouse’, ‘Mickey 17’, and ‘The Drama’.

Fans are divided but excited. Pattinson’s appeal comes not just from his handsomeness but from his ability to remain humble and lovably goofy as he has amassed major credits—no small feat from an actor who was mocked for years for appearing in the timelessly awkward ‘Twilight’ series. This seems to be the source of both the skepticism and the celebration surrounding today’s news. 

One X user said, “Robert Pattinson will kill it as Bond, no question but it’s a decision that’s definitely influenced by Hollywood’s lack of faith in an audience’s ability to attach to a new face.” 

Others have already begun to look past Pattinson’s casting to begin speculating on who will play his arch-nemesis. There is really only one name being thrown around, and she’s been seen on screen with Pattinson before: 

“Kristen Stewart as a Bond villain would be so cunt,” another X user posted. 

For Pattinson, there are definitely some challenges ahead. And there are some good reasons to wonder how the actor was chosen over Idris Elba or Callum Turner who fans had hoped might bag the role. But isn’t Bond known for catching us off-guard? For appearing where we’d least expect him to appear?

The luxury world has lost one of its most influential jewellery figures. Paolo Bulgari, the Italian entrepreneur and former chairman of Bvlgari, has passed away at the age of 89. 

As the grandson of founder Sotirio Bulgari, he played a defining role in transforming the family’s jewellery business, established in Rome in 1884, into one of the world’s most prestigious luxury houses. 

Under his creative leadership, Bvlgari became renowned for its bold use of coloured gemstones, distinctive gold designs and creations inspired by Rome’s artistic heritage. His influence extended beyond jewellery, helping the brand expand internationally before its acquisition by LVMH in 2011. 

Beyond his business legacy, he also founded the Paolo Bulgari Foundation in 2019 to support education and disadvantaged communities in Rome. His passing marks the end of an important chapter in the history of Italian luxury.

“Human” was announced as Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year for 2026 on Tuesday. In the age of artificial intelligence, the low-tech word stands out. 

Editors of the dictionary aim to capture the zeitgeist with their decision, examining online searches and looking at “collocation,” which refers to instances in which one word is paired with another. Terms like “human governance,” “human offered,” “human written” and “human need” were coming up often, Jessica Rundell, the dictionary’s commissioning editor, said.

People might have made those searches wondering whether their jobs would exist in a few months. Or maybe in the middle of sleepless nights, haunted by warnings from the creators of A.I.

“Maybe language is the best resistance we have; maybe if we say ‘human’ often enough the bots will not own us,” the New York Times reporter Ginia Bellefante writes. At the link in our bio, read more about what “human” means in 2026.

Around 1,000 women farmers across 25 villages in Maharashtra’s Sindhudurg district have adopted the System of Rice Intensification (SRI), a farming method that has increased rice yields by approximately 58% compared to conventional cultivation.

Supported through the UNDP’s climate resilience project, the initiative helps women farmers tackle challenges such as rising labour costs, fertiliser expenses and unpredictable rainfall. SRI involves planting younger seedlings individually with wider spacing, along with improved water and nutrient management.

Field trials recorded an average yield of 55.2 kg per 100 square metres using SRI, compared to 34.9 kg through traditional methods. The initiative is also helping women farmers strengthen their collective decision-making and adapt to changing climate conditions.

Indian cinema loves a good love triangle. Three people, complicated feelings, questionable decisions, and eventually, someone getting their heart broken. But when queer desire enters the equation, the odds of that character getting a happy ending become considerably less favourable.

In Dostana, the suggestion of queerness is played for laughs. In Cobalt Blue, two siblings fall for the same man, but their relationships with him exist under very different social conditions. Meanwhile, films such as Badhaai Do and Kaathal – The Core complicate the idea that marriage is the inevitable destination of romance.

And then there are Loev and Kuch Sapney Apne, where queer characters get to experience jealousy, betrayal, and the ordinary messiness of love.
So is Indian cinema finally ready to stop playing straight favourites?

The death of Divyanshu Joshi, a 26-year-old model and retail associate at fashion design brand Kartik Research, in a drowning accident at a quarry in Kerala on May 28 this year, became, in the days that followed, a flashpoint for debate in the fashion industry. This personal tragedy for Joshi’s family became the kind of controversy where allegations play endlessly on loop, acquiring hashtags that skew the facts. Kartik Kumra, designer and founder at Kartik Research, was criticised over the circumstances surrounding the incident, including questions about the safety protocols and insurance cover available to those working on fashion shoots. 𝑻𝑽𝑶𝑭 ran a story too, on the lack of safety measures and insurance for those who work in the Indian fashion industry. A statement from Kumra’s brand was also cited. 
On 30 July 2026, the Kerala Police closed the investigation, classifying Joshi’s death as “accidental drowning; no person has been charged or named as a suspect. The investigation’s finding established that Joshi had entered the water at the Pettamala quarry on his initiative to swim recreationally, removed his clothing and asked a colleague to record it (through photos and video). He drowned when his foot slipped off the rock he was holding on to. The report expressly records that his death did not occur during any shoot activity.” Earlier this week, the Kerala district court’s closure report on the case was finally made public. 𝑻𝑽𝑶𝑭 has access to the police document.
We had reached out to Kumra months ago, seeking to establish his account of the events and the aftermath. In this exclusive, recorded over two interviews, he recounts what happened, questions the media’s handling of the story and considers the industry’s responsibilities towards its workers. The conversation that was waiting for the court’s closure report, also moves to a concrete response: the first-ever insurance initiative in the Indian fashion industry that Kumra has helped develop with the Fashion Design Council of India (FDCI). Prince William landed in Mumbai and, somewhere between royal protocol and gully cricket, made a very good case for Indian menswear. For his first public engagement, the Prince of Wales stepped out in a navy sleeveless Nehru jacket by Rikki Kher’s Delhi-based label Kardo. Understated, sharply cut and unmistakably textile-led, it is exactly the kind of piece that explains why Kardo—and Indian menswear at large—is having such a compelling moment. While Kher maintains a polite “no comment” when we ask him who placed the order, he does clarify that the jacket was part of the original order, not a last-minute addition, as reported. 
The deceptively simple jacket, priced at ₹17,500, conceals an interesting textile engineering feat. Developed with GlocalWeaves’ textile engineer Fatima Radiowala and the artisan communities she works with, the fabric draws on the Jamdani supplementary-weft tradition, with its typically lightweight weave “tripled in weight” for menswear heft. Handwoven in Harali, West Bengal, by Netai Mana and Brojokishore Maity, a 12-metre thaan takes around 15 days to weave. 
That textile-first approach has been Kardo’s calling card since the London-born designer founded the label in 2013. Kher adroitly marries handloom, khadi, Ikat, block printing, bandhani and embroidery with workwear and military-derived silhouettes. Under the brand’s ONExONE system, one tailor cuts, sews and finishes each garment, and is named on its label.
Interestingly, at the Earthshot Prize Awards ceremony held later last evening, CEO Jason Knauf—Kher’s “personal friend”—wore a Kardo jacket fashioned from a vintage kantha blanket, over-embroidered with suzani threadwork. “We’ve been working with kantha blankets for a while, designing them into contemporary menswear… silhouettes you wouldn’t expect from such a textile,” says Kher, adding that Anna Wintour, global editorial director, Vogue magazine, “loved the jacket and commented on it”.
With the Nehru jacket available online in other colourways, between the extra-weft cotton and kantha-suzani combination, Kardo is clearly making a persuasive case for craft-led menswear.

Five characters, one @michelleyeoh_official. The Oscar-winning actress joked that she was “tricked” into taking on five different roles in “Sandiwara,” the 11-minute film directed by Sean Baker for Self-Portrait’s residency project.⁠
⁠
Set in Penang, Malaysia, the film follows Yeoh as five women with distinct personalities and appearances, from a hawker market chef to a pink-haired vlogger, a free-spirit waitress, a discerning critic and a self-conscious singer.⁠
⁠
Fashion helped Yeoh build each role. The clothes, hair and makeup gave her a way into each character, alongside the way she walked, slouched or spoke. @mrselfportrait founder Han Chong said the clothes were meant to support Yeoh’s performance, rather than take attention away from it.⁠
⁠

@kyliejenner is bringing @khy into the physical retail world for the first time.⁠
⁠
The digitally native fashion brand, which Jenner founded in 2023, will open the “Khy I <3 LA Pop-up” at 8580 Sunset Boulevard in West Hollywood from Dec. 4 to 13. The pop-up will be open daily from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., with no reservations required.⁠
⁠
“It feels so surreal,” Jenner told WWD in a statement.⁠
⁠
The opening follows a refresh of the brand earlier this year with its Born in L.A. collection, which introduced a new logo, revamped website and visual identity.⁠

⁠
The 18-year-old daughter of @nicolerichie and Good Charlotte frontman @joelmadden was born Harlow Winter Kate Madden, but she has gone by Kate since childhood.⁠

In ancient Egypt, the practice of mummification extended far beyond human remains. Animals occupied a significant place within the religious and funerary landscape, serving as sacred manifestations of deities, votive offerings and, in certain instances, companions accompanying the deceased into the afterlife.

Birds, cats, dogs, crocodiles, snakes and other creatures were mummified in vast numbers, often in association with particular gods. Animal mummies were deposited in temple precincts and dedicated catacombs, reflecting the complex relationship between religious devotion, ritual practice and the natural world.

Together, these objects and investigations offer a glimpse into an ancient understanding of the relationship between humans, animals, divinity and the afterlife.

The United Nations' highest court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, nearly a decade after a brutal military crackdown in 2017. Thousands were killed, villages were burned, and more than 700,000 people fled to neighbouring Bangladesh, where many still live in refugee camps.

The case was brought by The Gambia, a small West African country, in 2019. After seven years of legal proceedings, the court found that Myanmar's military had acted with the intention of destroying part of the Rohingya population. 

Why does this matter? 

For the first time in its history, the International Court of Justice has found a country responsible for committing genocide. The court also ordered Myanmar to investigate those responsible, allow displaced Rohingya to return safely, and provide compensation. Whether these orders will be carried out remains uncertain.

For the Rohingya, it is a historic moment: 
after years of displacement, denial and demands for justice, the world's highest court has formally recognized that what happened to them was genocide

If you want to learn more, check out episode 61 of the @brownhistorypodcast where we explore the haunting question: how the world failed the Rohingya?

Voyager 1 left Earth in 1977 to fly past Jupiter and Saturn. Nearly fifty years later, it’s the furthest human-made object from Earth and the first to reach one light-day away. A radio signal takes 24 hours to get there. NASA put a copy of the Golden Record aboard each Voyager in case anyone ever found it. The gold-plated disc holds whale calls, human laughter, music and greetings in 55 languages. Among them are Gujarati, Kannada, Punjabi and other South Asian languages. Those voices are still travelling through interstellar space.

Every Diwali, the debate over fireworks turns into a clash over faith, memory, and the right to celebrate. Because firecrackers feel so central to the festival, questioning them is often seen as an attack on Hindu tradition. Yet how old is this tradition, really?

Diwali’s connection to lamps stretches back millennia, while fireworks entered Indian celebrations much later. Today, that history sits at the center of a difficult tension between nostalgia and modern reality, especially as this year’s Diwali pushed Delhi’s AQI to 376, its worst in five years. Even with rising pollution concerns, calls to limit fireworks continue to provoke fierce debates over religion and identity. If traditions have always evolved with changing times, why should adapting them now feel like a betrayal?

In the latest Brown History Newsletter, Nishad Sanzagiri traces the surprising history of Diwali fireworks and explores how they became such a fiercely defended tradition.
